title: Work and learning languages
title_target: 무슨 일 하세요 — Museun il haseyo
goal: Talk about your job and your learning history — and use the duration word 동안, which hasn't appeared until now.
bekal: asking about and naming jobs politely
saying how long you've been learning something
using -기 전에 and -(으)ㄴ 후에 to order events in time

dialogs.title: 대화 — Introductions at a work event
dialogs.intro: Ani meets one of Minjun's colleagues. Notice that this conversation uses more formal forms than earlier units, because the two have just met in a work setting.

lines.speaker: 박 과장:
lines.id: Nice to meet you. I'm Park Minsu.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Hello. My name is Ani. I look forward to working with you.
lines.literal: hello. Ani — as — am-called. well — humbly-request.

lines.speaker: 박 과장:
lines.literal: Ani — Ms. — as-for — what — work — do (honorific)?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: I work at a café. And I'm at university.
lines.literal: café-at — work. and — university-to — attending — am.

lines.speaker: 박 과장:
lines.id: You must be busy. How long have you been learning Korean?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: I've been learning for a year. I'm still not very good.
lines.literal: one-year — during — learned. still — well — can't-do.

lines.speaker: 박 과장:
lines.id: Not at all, you're very good. Did you study before coming to Korea?
lines.literal: no, very — good-at (honorific) — though. Korea-to — coming — before — learned?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Yes, I studied for six months in Indonesia.
lines.literal: yes, Indonesia-in — six — months — during — studied.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: I want to work at a Korean company. That's why I study hard.
lines.literal: Korea — company-at — work — want. so — diligently — study.

lines.speaker: 박 과장:
lines.id: That's a great idea. Get in touch after you graduate.
lines.literal: good — thought — is. graduate — after — contact — give.

notes: **무슨 일 하세요? is the standard way to ask about someone's job.** Literally "what work do you do?". ⚠️ Don't ask 직업이 뭐예요? ("what is your occupation?") — it's grammatically correct but sounds like an immigration officer filling in a form.

**동안 means "for / during" and goes after the length of time.** 일년 **동안** = for one year. 세 시간 **동안** = for three hours. ⚠️ Don't confuse it with 에, which marks a point in time: 세 시**에** (at three o'clock) is completely different from 세 시간 **동안** (for three hours).

**얼마나 배웠어요? means "how long have you been learning?"** Note that Korean uses the **past** form for something still going on now, where English uses "have been learning". Different tense, same idea: the learning started in the past.
**아니라고 합니다 means "my name is Ani" in a very polite form.** Literally "I am called Ani". It sounds more modest than 아니입니다 and is common in work introductions.

**부탁드립니다 is a more respectful form of 부탁합니다.** 드리다 is the humble form of 주다 (to give) — used when you give something to someone higher up. It's the mirror image of 시: where 시 raises the other person, 드리다 lowers yourself, for the same effect.

**Job titles are used as forms of address, instead of names.** 박 과장(님) means "Section Chief Park". In a Korean office, calling a superior by name alone almost never happens; you use surname + title + 님. Common titles: 사장님 (company president), 부장님 (department head), 과장님 (section chief), 대리 (assistant manager).

**The -겠- in 바쁘시겠어요 expresses a caring guess.** It isn't just "you must be busy" — it also acknowledges the other person's situation. This form is very common for showing empathy: 힘드시겠어요 (that must be hard), 피곤하시겠어요 (you must be tired).

**Deflecting praise still applies here.** When praised with 잘하시는데요, Ani answers modestly. Notice that Park also opens his reply with 아니에요 — rejecting Ani's low opinion of herself. Denials going both ways like this are completely normal.

grammars.title: Duration with 동안
body: It goes after the span of time, and only for **how long** — not for when.
after: ⚠️ **Months have two words that must not be mixed up.** **달** and **개월** count months (여섯 달, 육 개월); **월** names a month (유월 = June). 육월 동안 is not a sentence.
**For ongoing activities, 동안 can be dropped:** 일년 배웠어요 is perfectly natural. It's only required when the sentence could be misread as a point in time.

grammars.title: Order in time: before and after
body: Two patterns that turn a verb into a time expression. Both use words you know from unit 15: 전에 and 후에.
after: **-기 전에 never changes form** — it's always 기, whatever the stem ends in. The easiest pattern in the whole book.
**-(으)ㄴ 후에 uses the (으)ㄴ pattern**, the same as the adjective modifier in unit 9: ㄴ after a vowel, 은 after a consonant.
**Tense is marked on the last verb of the sentence, not on the time expression:** 한국에 오기 전에 공부**했**어요. 오기 stays in its basic form even though the event is in the past.

blocks.text: **아르바이트** comes from German *Arbeit* by way of Japanese, and is shortened to **알바** in conversation. It means a part-time job, not a permanent one — and it's what almost every university student in Korea does.

head: Sentence
Meaning
rows: How long have you been learning Korean?
I've been learning for a year.
I've been learning since last year.
I studied a little before coming to Korea.
Listening is easy, but speaking is hard.
I want to work at a Korean company.
I'm going to take the TOPIK exam.

blocks.title: 듣기, 말하기, 읽기, 쓰기
items: The ending **-기** turns a verb into a noun: 듣다 → 듣기 (listening), 말하다 → 말하기 (speaking), 읽다 → 읽기 (reading), 쓰다 → 쓰기 (writing).
These four are the official names of the TOPIK exam sections, and you'll see them in every Korean textbook.
The same pattern makes nouns from other verbs: 요리하기 (cooking), 운동하기 (exercising), 사진 찍기 (taking photos) — very handy for naming hobbies.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: 무슨 일 하세요? — 카페에서 일해요. — 한국어를 얼마나 배웠어요? — 일년 동안 배웠어요. — 아직 잘 못해요. — 한국 회사에서 일하고 싶어요.
